items.bodyEn: Ōiso sits right on Sagami Bay, and stretches of its old Tōkaidō pine avenue still stand. Hiroshige titled his print Ōiso: Tora's Rain, after the seasonal rain of the fifth lunar month that tradition linked to the tears of Tora Gozen, mourning Soga Jūrō after the Soga brothers' revenge of 1193.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō series (c. 1833), print 'Ōiso: Tora ga Ame' (虎ヶ雨)

items.bodyEn: Sea bathing came to Japan as medicine. In 1885 the army surgeon Matsumoto Jun, trained in Dutch medicine, promoted Ōiso's Terugasaki beach as a health cure, making it one of the country's first official bathing beaches. Statesmen and writers soon built villas here, and the fishing town became a seaside retreat.

The counter 〜本 counts long, thin things: pencils, bottles, umbrellas, trees. Japanese then extends the image to anything felt as a line through time or space: phone calls, train lines, films, home runs, bus routes. So a movie and a bottle of water share a counter. Watch the sound changes: 一本 ippon, 三本 sanbon, 六本 roppon.
items.ja: ペンが{三本|さんぼん}あります。
items.kana: ペンがさんぼんあります。

items.bodyEn: The native counters ひとつ, ふたつ and the rest hide an ancient pattern. In Old Japanese, doubling a number was marked by changing its vowel: hito (1) and futa (2), mi (3) and mu (6), yo (4) and ya (8). Linguists treat these pairs as fossils of a counting system older than the borrowed Chinese numerals いち, に, さん.
items.sourceNote: Nihon Kokugo Daijiten (Shōgakukan), entries ひとつ・みつ・よつ; Old Japanese numerals
